Notes: C#- OOP-I

OOP-I

C# is an object-oriented programming (OOP) language, which means that it supports the concepts of classes and objects, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism.

A class is a blueprint for creating objects (a particular data structure), providing initial values for state (member variables or attributes), and implementations of behavior (member functions or methods).

An object is an instance of a class and is created at runtime. Objects have their own state and behavior, and they interact with other objects through methods.

Encapsulation is the practice of keeping the internal state and behavior of an object hidden from the outside world. This is achieved in C# through the use of access modifiers such as private, protected, and internal.

Inheritance is the ability of a class to inherit properties and methods from a parent class. This allows for a hierarchical relationship between classes and allows for code reuse.

Polymorphism is the ability of a single method or property to be used by objects of different classes. This is achieved in C# through the use of interfaces and virtual methods.

C# also supports the concept of abstract classes and interfaces, which are used to define the structure and behavior of a group of related classes.

It also supports generics which is a way to design classes and methods that work with multiple types.

Overall, C#'s object-oriented features allow for the creation of organized, reusable, and maintainable code.

class

​A class is a user-defined blueprint or prototype from which objects are created. Basically, a class combines the fields and methods(member function which defines actions) into a single unit. 

Syntax:
[access-modifier] class identifier [:base-class]
{
    class-body
}

Modifiers: A class can be public or internal etc. By default modifier of the class is internal.
Keyword class: A class keyword is used to declare the type class.
Class Identifier: The variable of type class is provided. The identifier(or name of the class) should begin with an initial letter which should be capitalized by convention.
Base class or Super class: The name of the class’s parent (superclass), if any, preceded by the : (colon). This is optional.
Body: The class body is surrounded by { } (curly braces).

public class Student //Class Name
{
      // Properties of a class
      public string Name{ get; set; }
      public int RollNumber{get; set; }

     public Student()
    {
        //Constructor
    }
}
object
​​​​​​​An object is an instance of a class. 
It is a basic unit of Object-Oriented Programming and represents real-life entities. 
An object consists of : 
State: It is represented by attributes of an object. It also reflects the properties of an object.
Behavior: It is represented by the methods of an object. It also reflects the response of an object with other objects.
Identity: It gives a unique name to an object and enables one object to interact with other objects.

​​​​​​​Creating an Object of a class
ClassName obj = new ClassName(); //syntax
Student st= new Student()
Access Specifiers
  1. public: The type or member can be accessed by any other code in the same assembly or another assembly that references it. 
  2. private: The type or member can be accessed only by code in the same class or struct.
  3. protected: The type or member can be accessed only by code in the same class, or in a class that is derived from that class.
  4. internal: The type or member can be accessed by any code in the same assembly, but not from another assembly. In other words, internal types or members can be accessed from code that is part of the same compilation.
  5. protected internal: The type or member can be accessed by any code in the assembly in which it's declared, or from within a derived class in another assembly.
  6. private protected: The type or member can be accessed by types derived from the class that are declared within its containing assembly. 

​
Fields
​​​​​​
  1. A class can have one or more fields.
  2. It is a class-level variable that holds a value. 
  3. A class or struct may have instance fields, static fields, or both. Instance fields are specific to an instance of a type. 
  4. Fields should not be accessed directly but always through Properties.
  5. The default access modifier is private.
    class Student{
    public int id;
    }

Static Field
​​They are also known as class static fields, static class variables or static member data.
  1. These are useful when you want to define a value that applies to all objects of a given type.
  2. Often used to keep a count of the number of objects that have been instantiated.
  3. Often used to store a value that must be shared among all the instances.
    class Counter {
    // Static field to count the number of instances
    public static int instanceCount = 0;
    }
    You can access static variables using class name only.
    e.g. Counter.instanceCount
Properties
  1. In C#, properties are a way to encapsulate the internal state of an object and provide a way to access and modify that state. Properties are typically used to expose the internal fields of a class and provide a way to read and write their values.
  2. Properties are the special type of class members that provides a flexible mechanism to read, write, or compute the value of a private field.
  3.  Properties can be used as if they are public data members, but they are actually special methods called accessors.
  4. This enables data to be accessed easily and helps to promote the flexibility and safety of methods. 
  5. Encapsulation and hiding of information can also be achieved using properties.
  6. It uses pre-defined methods which are “get” and “set” methods which help to access and modify the properties. 

Accessors: The block of “set” and “get” is known as “Accessors”. It is very essential to restrict the accessibility of property.
 There are two type of accessors i.e. get accessors and set accessors. 
  1. There are different types of properties based on the “get” and “set” accessors:
    • Read and Write Properties: When property contains both get and set methods.
    • Read-Only Properties: When property contains only get method.
    • Write Only Properties: When property contains only set method.
    • Auto Implemented Properties: When there is no additional logic in the property accessors and it introduce in C# 3.0.
get, set 
 The syntax for Defining Properties:
<access_modifier> <return_type> <property_name>
{
        get { // body }
        set { // body }
}
Where, <access_modifier> can be public, private, protected or internal.
Access modifiers define how users of the class can access the property. 
<return_type> can be any valid C# type.
<property_name> can be user-defined. 
Example:
class Student
    {
        private int _Id;
        public int Id { 
            get { return _Id;  }
            set { _Id = value; }
        }
    }

From C# 3.0 onwards, property declaration has been made easy if you don't want to apply some logic in getter or setter. 
Using auto-implemented property, you don't need to declare an underlying private field.
 C# compiler will automatically create it in IL code.
Example:
class Student
    {
        public string FirstName { get; set; }
        public string LastName { get; set; }
    }

You can initialize auto-implemented properties similarly to fields
Example:
public string FirstName { get; set; } = "Jane";
Read only properties

In C#, read-only properties are properties that can only be read, not written to. They can be used to provide read-only access to the internal state of an object.

A read-only property is declared using the get accessor and omitting the set accessor. Here is an example of a read-only property in C#: 

class Example
{
    private int _value;

    public int Value
    {
        get { return _value; }
    }
}
In this example, the Value property is read-only because it only has a get accessor and not a set accessor. The _value field is used to store the internal state of the object, and the get accessor of the Value property returns the value of this field.
You can also create read-only properties using readonly field
class Example
{
    public readonly int Value;
    public Example(int value)
    {
        Value = value;
    }
}
In this example, the Value property is read-only because it is defined as a readonly field. The field is initialized in the constructor of the class. 

Read-only properties are useful when you want to ensure that the state of an object cannot be modified by external code, or when you want to provide read-only access to an internal state that is calculated or derived from other properties.

Constructors
​​​​​​​A constructor is a special method of the class which gets automatically invoked whenever an instance of the class is created. 
Like methods, a constructor also contains the collection of instructions that are executed at the time of Object creation. 
It is used to assign initial values to the data members of the same class. 
Example:
class Student
    {
        public Student() {
            //Constructor
        }
    }

  1. Constructor of a class must have the same name as the class name in which it resides.
  2. A constructor can not be abstract, final, and Synchronized.
  3. Within a class, you can create only one static constructor.
  4. A constructor doesn’t have any return type, not even void.
  5. A static constructor cannot be a parameterized constructor.
  6. A class can have any number of constructors.
  7. Access modifiers can be used in constructor declaration to control its access i.e which other class can call the constructor. 
  8. A class can have multiple constructors with different parameters but can only have one parameter less constructor.
  9. If no constructor is defined, the C# compiler would create it internally.

​

Example:
class Student
    {
        private int id;
        private string name;
        private string email;
        private string phone;

        //Default Constructor
        public Student()
        {
            this.id = default;
            this.name = string.Empty;
            this.email = string.Empty;
            this.phone = string.Empty;
        }

        //Parametrised Constructor
        public Student(int id, string name, string email, string phone)
        {
            this.id = id;
            this.name = name;
            this.email = email;
            this.phone = phone;
        }

        //Copy Constructor
        public Student(Student s)
        {
            this.id = s.id;
            this.name = s.name;
            this.email = s.email;
            this.phone = s.phone;
        }
    }

Private Constructor
If a constructor is created with private specifier is known as Private Constructor. It is not possible for other classes to derive from this class and also it’s not possible to create an instance of this class. 

Points To Remember :  
  1. It is the implementation of a singleton class pattern.
  2. use private constructor when we have only static members.
  3. Using private constructor, prevents the creation of the instances of that class.

Example:
class Student
    {
        //Private Constructor 
        private Student() {
            //Constructor
        }
    }

Destructors
​​​​​​​Destructors in C# are methods inside the class used to destroy instances of that class when they are no longer needed. The Destructor is called implicitly by the .NET Framework’s Garbage collector and therefore programmer has no control as when to invoke the destructor. An instance variable or an object is eligible for destruction when it is no longer reachable.

Important Points:
  1. A Destructor is unique to its class i.e. there cannot be more than one destructor in a class.
  2. A Destructor has no return type and has exactly the same name as the class name (Including the same case).
  3. It is distinguished apart from a constructor because of the Tilde symbol (~) prefixed to its name.
  4. A Destructor does not accept any parameters and modifiers.
  5. It cannot be defined in Structures. It is only used with classes.
  6. It cannot be overloaded or inherited.
  7. It is called when the program exits.
  8. Internally, Destructor called the Finalize method on the base class of object.​​​​​​​
    class Example
    { 
        // Rest of the class
        // members and methods.
        // Destructor
       ~Example()
        {
            // Your code
        }
    } 

Object Initializer
In C#, object initializers are a way to create and initialize an object in a single statement. An object initializer is a list of one or more member initializers, enclosed in curly braces, that follow an object creation expression.

Example of using an object initializer to create and initialize an instance of a class:
class Point
{
    public int X { get; set; }
    public int Y { get; set; }
}
Point point = new Point { X = 1, Y = 2 };

In this example, a new instance of the Point class is created, and its X and Y properties are set to 1 and 2, respectively. The object initializer syntax eliminates the need to create a separate statement to set the property values after the object has been created.

You can also use object initializer to initialize the collection as well:

List<int> numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };

You can also use object initializer for collection initializer, nested object initializer and for Anonymous types as well.

var person = new Person { Name = "John", Age = 25 };
Object initializers can make your code more readable and concise. They also enable you to create and initialize an object in a single step, without having to create separate statements for object creation and property initialization.
C# 3.0 (.NET 3.5) introduced Object Initializer Syntax, a new way to initialize an object of a class or collection.
 Object initializers allow you to assign values to the fields or properties at the time of creating an object without invoking a constructor.
Example:
public class Student
    {
        public int Id { get; set; }
        public string Name { get; set; }
        public string Email { get; set; }
        public string Address { get; set; }
    }

    public class Program {
        static void Main(string[] args)
        {
            Student st = new Student()
            {
                Id = 10,
                Name = "Snehal",
                Email = "snehal.test@gmail.com",
                Address = "Pune"
            };
        }
    }
Collection initializer Syntax
public class Student
    {
        public int Id { get; set; }
        public string Name { get; set; }
        public string Email { get; set; }
        public string Address { get; set; }
    }

    public class Program {

            };
            
        }

​​​​​​​Advantages of Initializers
  • Code conciseness: Initializers can reduce the number of lines of code needed to initialize an object and its properties.
  • Code readability: Initializers can make code easier to read.
  • Multi-threading: Initializers are useful in multi-threading.
  • Module initialization: Module initialization can help avoid deadlocking and startup race conditions.
  • Collection elements: Initializers make it easier to add elements to collections.
  • Anonymous objects: Initializers can create anonymous objects
Methods
  • A method can contain one or more statements to be executed as a single unit. 
  • A method may or may not return a value. A method can have one or more input parameters.
Syntax
[access-modifier] return-type MethodName(type parameterName1, type parameterName2,...) { }

Example: 
public int Sum(int num1, int num2) 
{ 
 var total = num1 + num2;
 return total;
 }

Optional Parameters
  • By default, all parameters of a method are required.  But in C# 4.0, the concept of optional parameters was introduced that allows developers to declare parameters as optional. 
  • That means, if these arguments are not passed, they will be omitted from the execution. Optional parameters are not mandatory.

Example:
public static int AddNumber(int firstNo, int secondNo=5)
        { 
            return firstNo + secondNo;
        }

        static void Main(string[] args)
        {
            Console.WriteLine(AddNumber(10));
            Console.WriteLine(AddNumber(10,30));
        }
Output:
15
40
Named Parameters
  1. Named Parameters allow developers  to pass a method arguments with parameter names. 
  2. Prior to these this feature, the method parameters were passed using a sequence only. Now, using named parameters in C#, we can put any parameter in any sequence as long as the name is there.
  3.  The right parameter value based on their names will be mapped to the right variable. The parameters name must match with the method definition parameter names. 

The syntax of parameter names is (parametername: value). 

Example: 
public static int AddNumber(int firstNo, int secondNo=5)
        { 
            return firstNo + secondNo;
        }

        static void Main(string[] args)
        {
            Console.WriteLine(AddNumber(firstNo:10,secondNo:20));
            Console.WriteLine(AddNumber(firstNo: 30));
            Console.WriteLine(AddNumber( secondNo: 20, firstNo: 23));
        }		Output:
30
35
43
Positional Parameters
  • C# supports the use of named arguments, in which you can change the order of arguments passed to a function, by prefixing an argument with the corresponding parameter name.
  • An argument that is not prefixed with the name of a parameter is considered a positional argument.
  • Positional arguments must come before named arguments and match the order of the corresponding parameters.

Example:
// Sample method with 3 parameters
    public void Bark(int numTimes, string sound, double volume)
 
Examples of using both named and positional arguments.
// Example 1: All arguments are positional
    myDog.Bark(2, "Woof", 10.0);
 
// Example 2: Only 1st argument is positional
    myDog.Bark(2, volume: 10.0, sound: "Woof"); 
Using params
  1. It is useful when the programmer doesn’t have any prior knowledge about the number of parameters to be used.  
  2. By using params you are allowed to pass any variable number of arguments.
  3.  Only one params keyword is allowed and no additional Params will be allowed in function declaration after a params keyword. 
  4. The length of params will be zero if no arguments will be passed.

Example:
using System;

class Program
{
    static void Main()
    {
        // Calling the method with different numbers of arguments
        DisplayNumbers(1, 2, 3);
        DisplayNumbers(4, 5, 6, 7, 8);
        DisplayNumbers(); // Calling with no arguments
    }

    // Method that uses the params keyword to take a variable number of integers
    static void DisplayNumbers(params int[] numbers)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("The numbers are:");
        if (numbers.Length == 0)
        {
            Console.WriteLine("No numbers provided");
        }
        else
        {
            foreach (int num in numbers)
            {
                Console.Write(num + " ");
            }
            Console.WriteLine();
        }
        Console.WriteLine();
    }
}​​​​​​
Outrput:
The numbers are:
1 2 3

The numbers are:
4 5 6 7 8

The numbers are:
No numbers provided
Local functions
  1. The local function feature is introduced in C# 7.0.
  2. It allows you to declare a method inside the body of an already defined method. 
  3. Or in other words, we can say that a local function is a private function of a function whose scope is limited to that function in which it is created. 
  4. The type of local function is similar to the type of function in which it is defined. 
  5. You can only call the local function from their container members. 

Important Points about Local Functions:
  1. Local functions are declared inside methods, constructors, property accessors, event accessors, anonymous methods, lambda expressions, finalizers, and other local functions.
  2. You cannot declare a local function in the expression-bodied member.
  3. Local function makes your program more readable and also save you from mistakenly call method because you cannot call a local function directly.
  4. In local function, you are allowed to use async and unsafe modifiers.
  5. Local function can access the local variables that are defined inside the container method including method parameters.
  6. You are not allowed to use any member access modifiers in the local function definition, including private keyword because they are by default private and you are not allowed to make them public.
  7. You are also not allowed to use static keyword with local function.
  8. You are also not allowed to apply attributes to the local function, or to its parameters, or to its parameter type.
  9. Multiple local functions are allowed.
  10. Overloading is not allowed for local functions.

Example:
using System;

class Program
{
    static void Main()
    {
        int result = Calculate(5, 7);
        Console.WriteLine("Result: " + result);
    }

    static int Calculate(int a, int b)
    {
        // Local function within the Calculate method
        int Add(int x, int y)
        {
            return x + y;
        }

        // Using the local function to perform addition
        int sum = Add(a, b);

        // You can perform more complex calculations here using other local functions if needed

        return sum;
    }
}		Output:
Result: 12
Project References
  1. A project reference is a link from the current Studio project to another project. 
  2. The reference makes certain resources in the referenced project become available for use in the current project. 

How to Add a reference
  1. In Solution Explorer, right-click the References or Dependencies node, and then choose either Add Project Reference from the context menu. (You can right-click the project node and select Add from the fly-out menu to choose from these options, too.)
  2. Reference Manager opens and lists the available references by group.
  3. Select a reference to add, and then select OK.

Indexers
  1. An indexer is a special type of property that allows a class or a structure to be accessed like an array for its internal collection. 
  2. C# allows us to define custom indexers, generic indexers, and also overload indexers.
  3. An indexer can be defined the same way as property with this keyword and square brackets [].

Syntax:
public class MyClass
{
    // Define an indexer
    [access_modifier] [return_type] this[argument_list]
    {
        get
        {
            // Return value based on index
        }
        set
        {
            // Set value based on index
        }
    }
}
  • access_modifier: It can be public, private, protected or internal.
  • return_type: It can be any valid C# type.
  • this: It is the keyword which points to the object of the current class.
  • argument_list: This specifies the parameter list of the indexer.
    get{ } and set { }: These are the accessors.
    ​​​​​​​
Example:
using System;
    
    public class SampleClass
    {
        private string[] data = new string[5];

        // Indexer declaration
        public string this[int index]
        {
            get
            {
                if (index >= 0 && index < data.Length)
                    return data[index];
                else
                    return "Index out of range";
            }
            set
            {
                if (index >= 0 && index < data.Length)
                    data[index] = value;
                else
                    Console.WriteLine("Index out of range");
            }
        }

        //Overloaded Indexer
        public int this[string name]
        {
            get
            {
                int index = 0;

                while (index < data.Length)
                {
                    if (data[index] == name)
                    {
                        return index;
                    }
                    index++;
                }
                return index;
            }
        }
    }

    class Program
    {
        static void Main(string[] args)
        {
            SampleClass sample = new SampleClass();

            // Setting values using the indexer
            sample[0] = "Value at index 0";
            sample[1] = "Value at index 1";
            sample[2] = "Value at index 2";

            // Getting values using the indexer
            Console.WriteLine(sample[0]);
            Console.WriteLine(sample[1]);
            Console.WriteLine(sample[2]);

            // Trying to access an out-of-range index
            Console.WriteLine(sample[5]); // This will print "Index out of range"

            //using the second indexer with the string parameter
            Console.WriteLine(sample["Value at index 1"]);
        }
    }
Output:
Value at index 0
Value at index 1
Value at index 2
Index out of range
1

Important Points About IndexersImportant Points About Indexers
  1. There are two types of Indexers i.e. One Dimensional Indexer & MultiDimensional Indexer. The above discussed is One Dimensional Indexer.
  2. Indexers can be overloaded.
  3. These are different from Properties.
  4. This enables the object to be indexed in a similar way to arrays.
  5. A set accessor will always assign the value while the get accessor will return the value.
  6. “this” keyword is always used to declare an indexer.
  7. To define the value being assigned by the set indexer, ” value” keyword is used.
  8. Indexers are also known as the Smart Arrays or Parameterized Property in C#.
  9. Indexer can’t be a static member as it is an instance member of the class.
Difference between Indexers and Properties

Indexers
Properties
Indexers are created with this keyword.
Properties don't require this keyword.
Indexers are identified by signature.
Properties are identified by their names.
Indexers are accessed using indexes.
Properties are accessed by their names.
Indexer are instance member, so can't be static.
Properties can be static as well as instance members.
A get accessor of an indexer has the same formal parameter list as the indexer.
A get accessor of a property has no parameters.
A set accessor of an indexer has the same formal parameter list as the indexer,
in addition to the value parameter.
A set accessor of a property contains the implicit value parameter.
Example:
// C# program to illustrate the Indexer
    using System;

    // class declaration
    class IndexerCreation
    {

        // class members
        private string[] val = new string[3];

        // Indexer declaration 
        // public - access modifier
        // string - the return type of the Indexer
        // this - is the keyword having a parameters list
        public string this[int index]
        {

            // get Accessor retrieving the values stored in val[] array of strings
            get
            {
                return val[index];
            }

            // set Accessor setting the value at passed index of val
            set
            {
                // value keyword is used to define the value being assigned by the set indexer.
                val[index] = value;
            }
        }
    }

    // Driver Class
    class main
    {

        // Main Method
        public static void Main()
        {
            // creating an object of parent class which acts as primary address for using Indexer
            IndexerCreation ic = new IndexerCreation();

            // Inserting values in ic[] Here we are using the object of class as an array
            ic[0] = "C";
            ic[1] = "CPP";
            ic[2] = "CSHARP";

            Console.Write("Printing values stored in objects used as arrays\n");

            // printing values
            Console.WriteLine("First value = {0}", ic[0]);
            Console.WriteLine("Second value = {0}", ic[1]);
            Console.WriteLine("Third value = {0}", ic[2]);

        }
    }
}
Output:
Printing values stored in objects used as arrays
First value = C
Second value = CPP
Third value = CSHARP
